title: Saa ngapi? The Swahili clock, shifted by six hours
goal: Tell time the East African way, name the days and months, make plans to meet — and avoid being six hours late on day one.
bekal: count the hours from sunrise, not from midnight
*na nusu*, *na robo*, *kasoro robo* for parts of the hour
the seven day names and how to give a date

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Tunakutana lini?
dialogs.intro: Juma invites Budi to the beach. All that's left is to settle the time — and that's where the most typical East African misunderstanding is waiting.

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.text: Kesho tunakwenda ufuoni. Tunakutana saa ngapi?
lines.id: Tomorrow we're going to the beach. What time shall we meet?
lines.literal: tomorrow we-are-going at-beach. we-are-meeting-each-other hour how-many?

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.text: Saa tatu asubuhi. Jua bado si kali.
lines.id: Nine in the morning. The sun isn't fierce yet.
lines.literal: hour three morning. sun not-yet not sharp.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ngoja kidogo... saa tatu ni saa tisa kwa saa yangu?
lines.id: Wait a moment... is saa tatu nine o'clock on my clock?
lines.literal: wait a-little... hour three is hour nine at hour of-me?

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.text: Ndiyo! Sisi tunahesabu kutoka macheo ya jua.
lines.id: Yes! We count from the sunrise.
lines.literal: yes! we we-are-counting from rising of sun.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Aa, sasa ninaelewa. Saa sita ni adhuhuri, siyo?
lines.id: Ah, now I understand. Saa sita is noon, right?
lines.literal: ah, now I-am-understanding. hour six is midday, not-so?

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.text: Hasa! Na saa kumi na mbili jioni ni machweo.
lines.id: Exactly! And saa kumi na mbili in the evening is sunset.
lines.literal: exactly! and hour ten and two evening is setting.

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.text: Hapana, kesho ni Jumatano. Jumamosi kuna sherehe kubwa.
lines.id: No, tomorrow is Wednesday. On Saturday there's a big party.
lines.literal: no, tomorrow is Wednesday. Saturday there-is party big.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Okay. What time do we come back?

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.text: Saa kumi na moja na nusu, kabla ya giza.
lines.id: Half past five in the afternoon, before dark.
lines.literal: hour ten and one and half, before of darkness.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Haya basi! Tutaonana kesho saa tatu kamili.
lines.id: All right then! See you tomorrow at nine sharp.
lines.literal: okay then! will-we-see-each-other tomorrow hour three complete.

notes: **The clock misunderstanding is the classic newcomer story in East Africa.** If someone gives a time in Swahili, they almost certainly mean the Swahili count. If they give it in English, they almost certainly mean international time. One lifesaving sentence: *Saa tatu ya Kiswahili au ya kizungu?* — Swahili three o'clock or Western three o'clock?

**Hasa means "exactly; precisely".** A short word of praise that is nice to use when you finally understand something. Its cousins: *sawa kabisa* (absolutely right) and *ndiyo hivyo* (yes, just like that).
**Kamili means "complete; exact".** *Saa tatu kamili* = three o'clock sharp. Notice also *kabla ya* (before) and its partner *baada ya* (after) — both from Arabic, and both followed by *ya*.
**Siyo? at the end of a sentence means "right?".** It invites your partner to confirm, exactly like "isn't that so?" in English. Other forms with the same use: *je?* and *sivyo?*

**Kutana means "to meet" and already contains "each other".** The ending *-ana* means mutual action: *kuona* (to see) → *kuonana* (to see each other, i.e. to meet), *kupenda* → *kupendana* (to love each other), *kusaidia* → *kusaidiana* (to help each other). That is why *tutaonana* means "see you".

grammars.title: The Swahili clock: counting starts at sunrise
body: On the equator, the sun rises and sets at almost the same time all year: around 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. So Swahili counts the hours **from sunrise**. The first hour after sunrise is *saa moja* — and that is 7 a.m.
The practical rule in one sentence: **add or subtract six**.
after: The four parts of the day are **obligatory to mention**, because the numbers repeat twice a day: *asubuhi* (morning, until midday), *mchana* (afternoon, daytime), *jioni* (evening, roughly after 4 p.m.), *usiku* (night). *Saa mbili asubuhi* = 8 a.m.; *saa mbili usiku* = 8 p.m.
The fastest way to convert in your head: **if the international hour is over 6, subtract 6; if it's under 6, add 6**. 15:00 → 15 − 6 = *saa tisa*. 4:00 → 4 + 6 = *saa kumi*.

⚠️ The word *saa* has three meanings at once: a clock time (*saa tatu*), a clock as an object (*saa yangu* = my watch), and a length of time (*saa mbili* = two hours). Context separates them, and they almost never cause confusion.

grammars.title: Half, quarter, and minutes
body: Parts of the hour are attached with *na* (past) and *kasoro* (to) — the same construction as English "past" and "to".
after: *Nusu* (half) and *robo* (quarter) come straight from Arabic (*nisf* and *rub'*). *Dakika* means minute, *sekunde* means second.

For a length of time rather than a point in time, the same words are used: *saa mbili* (two hours), *dakika thelathini* (thirty minutes), *siku tatu* (three days), *wiki moja* (one week), *mwezi mmoja* (one month).
Asking about time: *Saa ngapi?* (what time is it?), *Saa ngapi tunakutana?* (what time do we meet?), *Lini?* (when?), *Kwa muda gani?* (for how long?).

sections.title: Siku za wiki — and why Monday is "day three"

blocks.text: Two names — **Alhamisi** and **Ijumaa** — come straight from Arabic. The rest are counted, and the count starts from **Jumamosi**: Saturday is day one of the week, Sunday is day two, Monday is day three (*Jumatatu*), Tuesday day four (*Jumanne*), Wednesday day five (*Jumatano*). What looks chaotic is actually consistent: the traditional Swahili week starts on Saturday.

Month names follow two patterns. The first is borrowed as is: *Januari, Februari, Machi, Aprili, Mei, Juni, Julai, Agosti, Septemba, Oktoba, Novemba, Desemba*. The second is counted: *mwezi wa kwanza* (first month = January), *mwezi wa pili*, and so on. Both are used; the counted version is heard more in the villages.
A date is given like this: *tarehe kumi na tano Machi* (the 15th of March). *Tarehe* is Arabic *tarikh*, "date".

sections.title: Jana, leo, kesho — placing yourself in time

blocks.text: *Alfajiri* and *adhuhuri* come from the names of the Muslim prayer times (Arabic *al-fajr*, *adh-dhuhr*). So does *magharibi* — in Swahili it means "west" and also "the time of sunset".

⚠️ One habit to be ready for: appointments in East Africa are kept loosely, and people joke about it themselves with the phrase *saa za Kiafrika* (African time). If precision matters, say *kamili* (exactly) and confirm again the day before. If it doesn't matter, just go with the rhythm — *haraka haraka haina baraka*.
